articles.title: PHP Dies After Every Request. How the Zend Engine Actually Runs Your Code.
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute architectural deep dive into how PHP actually executes under the hood. From the Shared-Nothing process model and OPcache bytecode caching to 16-byte zvals, Copy-on-Write, and the Tracing JIT.
articles.body_html:
For more than two decades, programmers coming from languages like Java, Python, Go, and Node.js have looked at PHP and repeated the exact same criticism:

"PHP does not even have a persistent application server. It boots up, runs a script, and dies after every single HTTP request. How could anyone build serious software on an architecture like that?"

The irony is that those critics missed the most profound design decision in modern web computing.

What looked like a primitive limitation was, in reality, a deliberate architectural choice called the Shared-Nothing Architecture.

While other language runtimes battle memory leaks that accumulate over weeks, global state that accidentally bleeds between concurrent users, and fatal unhandled exceptions that knock down entire server clusters, PHP operates on a radically different premise:

PHP executes in total isolation, reclaims every single byte of memory at the end of the request, and resets to a pristine blank slate.

Yet modern PHP is not slow. Over the last decade, the core engineering team completely rebuilt the runtime from the ground up:

  • The Zend Engine was rewritten with cache-optimized 16-byte zval structures.
  • OPcache eliminates file parsing by caching bytecode directly inside shared operating system memory.
  • Copy-on-Write ensures massive arrays consume zero extra RAM until mutated.
  • PHP 8's Tracing JIT compiles hot execution loops directly into native silicon machine code.

To truly understand why PHP powers over 75% of the web, you have to look beneath the surface syntax and examine how the Zend Engine and PHP-FPM actually execute your code under the hood.

Here is the complete journey of a PHP request.

The Shared-Nothing Philosophy: Why Dying on Purpose Is a Superpower

To appreciate the Zend Engine, you must first understand the architectural divide between long-lived persistent runtimes and PHP.

In Node.js, Python (FastAPI/Django), Ruby (Puma), and Go, your application boots once. The runtime initializes global variables, establishes database connection pools, loads framework classes, and starts an event loop or worker thread pool that lives for days or months.

This model is fast, but it carries profound architectural vulnerabilities:

  1. State Leaks Across Users: If a developer accidentally mutates a global object or attaches data to an uncleaned request context, User B can end up reading private data belonging to User A.
  2. Slow-Motion Memory Leaks: If a third-party package slowly appends items to a cache that never gets cleared, the process slowly exhausts RAM until an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates the process.
  3. Catastrophic Blast Radius: If an unhandled exception causes a fatal crash or memory corruption, the entire server process dies, severing thousands of active connections simultaneously.

PHP took the opposite path: The Shared-Nothing Process Model.

When an HTTP request arrives at a PHP worker:

  1. The worker allocates a fresh, completely isolated memory arena called the Request Heap (managed by Zend Memory Manager, ZendMM).
  2. Superglobals ($_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER) are populated freshly for that specific request.
  3. Your application executes in total isolation. No other concurrent user shares that memory space.
  4. The HTTP response headers and body are flushed to the web server.
  5. The Zend Engine instantly tears down the request heap. Every variable, object, database handle, and memory buffer is wiped out in a single sweep.
  6. The worker process returns to its pristine resting state, ready for the next request.

This design gives PHP an almost indestructible reliability.

Memory leaks simply cannot survive across requests. If a buggy piece of code allocates 50 megabytes of temporary data and forgets to clean it up, the Zend Engine sweeps it away automatically the instant the response finishes.

And if a script encounters a fatal error or segmentation fault, it kills only that single worker. The master process respawns a replacement in under a millisecond without dropping any other concurrent user request.

The Compilation Pipeline: From PHP Text to Zend Opcodes

A common misconception is that because PHP dies after every request, it must re-read and re-parse your .php files from disk every time someone loads a page.

In PHP 3 and 4, that was true. In modern PHP, that model has been dead for over a decade.

When PHP processes a file, it passes through four distinct phases:

[PHP File] ──> [Lexer: Tokens] ──> [Parser: AST] ──> [Compiler: Opcodes] ──> [Zend VM Executor]

1. Lexing (Tokenization)

The Zend Lexer scans your raw PHP script and converts the character stream into a sequence of language tokens (such as T_VARIABLE, T_OBJECT_OPERATOR, T_STRING).

2. Parsing (Abstract Syntax Tree)

Introduced in PHP 7, the Zend Parser reads the tokens and constructs a hierarchical Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). The AST validates syntax, resolves operator precedence, and organizes your program logic into a structured tree before code generation.

3. Compilation (Zend Opcodes)

The compiler walks the AST and emits Zend Opcodes. An opcode is a low-level virtual machine instruction, comparable to Java bytecode or Python bytecode.

For example, this simple addition:

$c = $a + $b;

compiles into low-level instructions that look like this:

ZEND_ADD      $a, $b, ~0
ZEND_ASSIGN   $c, ~0

4. The Game Changer: OPcache in Shared Memory

In a stock PHP installation without caching, compiling source files on every request would indeed create heavy CPU overhead.

This is where OPcache enters the picture.

OPcache intercepts the compilation pipeline. The first time a PHP file is loaded, OPcache compiles it into Zend Opcodes and stores the compiled bytecode directly inside Shared Memory (SHM).

When subsequent requests arrive:

  • PHP skips the Lexer entirely.
  • PHP skips the Parser and AST construction entirely.
  • PHP skips the Compiler entirely.

Instead, the Zend VM executor fetches the pre-compiled opcodes directly from memory and executes them immediately.

With Preloading (introduced in PHP 7.4 and standard in modern frameworks like Laravel and Symfony), frameworks can compile all core classes, traits, and interfaces on server boot into permanent shared memory.

When a user request hits your application, the entire framework is already resident in RAM, ready to execute with zero initialization latency.

The 16-Byte Miracle: How the Zend Engine Stores Variables

In PHP, a variable can be an integer, a floating-point number, a string, an array, an object, or null. It can change its type dynamically at runtime:

$x = 42;
$x = "Hello World";
$x = [1, 2, 3];

How does a statically-compiled C program (which the Zend Engine is) represent a dynamically-typed variable with minimal memory overhead?

The answer is the zval (Zend Value).

In PHP 5, a zval was a bloated C structure requiring 32 to 48 bytes on 64-bit systems. Worse, every single zval was allocated as an independent block on the heap, scattering pointers across memory and causing frequent CPU cache misses.

In PHP 7, core engineer Dmitry Stogov led a complete rewrite of the Zend Engine known as phpng (PHP Next Generation). The zval was completely redesigned into an ultra-compact, 16-byte structure.

Here is what a zval looks like under the hood in C:

struct _zval_struct {
    zend_value value;            /* 8 bytes: union holding primitive or pointer */
    union {
        struct {
            zend_uchar type;     /* 1 byte: IS_LONG, IS_STRING, IS_ARRAY, etc. */
            zend_uchar type_flags;
            zend_uchar const_flags;
            zend_uchar reserved;
        } v;
        uint32_t type_info;      /* 4 bytes total */
    } u1;
    union {
        uint32_t next;           /* hash collision chaining */
        uint32_t cache_slot;     /* literal cache */
        ...
    } u2;                        /* 4 bytes total */
};

Notice the engineering elegance of this layout:

  • Exactly 16 bytes total on any 64-bit architecture.
  • For primitive integers (IS_LONG) and floats (IS_DOUBLE), the number is stored directly inside the 8-byte value field. There is zero pointer indirection and zero heap allocation!
  • For complex types like strings (IS_STRING) or arrays (IS_ARRAY), the value field stores a pointer to a dedicated payload structure (zend_string or zend_array).
  • The zval itself is allocated directly on the CPU execution stack or embedded inside contiguous array memory. It does not require separate heap allocation calls.

This single refactoring doubled PHP's raw execution speed and cut memory consumption in half across the entire world on the day PHP 7 was released.

Copy-on-Write: The Art of Memory Laziness

Consider this PHP code:

$users = get_large_user_dataset(); // A massive 100,000-item array (~20 MB)
$backup = $users;                  // What happens here?

In many languages, assigning an array to a new variable either duplicates the entire array in memory (wasting 20 MB of RAM) or passes a mutable reference where changes to $backup mutate $users.

In PHP, arrays have value semantics: modifying $backup will never mutate $users.

Does that mean PHP duplicates 20 megabytes of memory on $backup = $users?

The answer is no, thanks to Copy-on-Write (COW).

Here is how Copy-on-Write works in the Zend Engine:

  1. Assignment without Duplication: When you write $backup = $users, PHP simply copies the 16-byte zval. Both $users and $backup point to the exact same physical zend_array in memory.
  2. Refcount Increment: PHP increments the array's reference counter: gc.refcount = 2. No array data is duplicated. The operation takes mere nanoseconds.
  3. The Mutation Trigger: As long as both variables only read from the array, they share the same physical memory block forever.
  4. Physical Separation: The moment you mutate one of the variables: 
$backup[0] = "Modified User";

The Zend Engine checks the refcount. Because refcount > 1, PHP knows that multiple variables point to this memory.

Only at that exact moment does PHP clone the array in memory, allocate a fresh block for $backup, decrement $users's refcount to 1, and apply the mutation to the new clone.

If you pass a 50-megabyte array through ten functions that only read data, PHP never duplicates that array once. You get the safety of pure pass-by-value semantics with the speed and efficiency of pass-by-reference pointers.

PHP-FPM: The Resilient Worker Pool

How does a web server like Nginx or Caddy communicate with PHP in production?

The bridge is PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager).

PHP does not run as an Apache module anymore. Modern production architectures run PHP as an independent daemon managing a pool of isolated worker processes.

The PHP-FPM architecture operates on a master-worker model:

  1. The Master Process: Runs as a privileged supervisor. It binds to a UNIX domain socket or TCP port, parses php.ini configurations, loads OPcache into shared memory, and spawns worker processes.
  2. The Worker Pool: A collection of pre-forked worker processes that listen for incoming FastCGI connections.
  3. Request Distribution: When Nginx receives an HTTP request for a .php endpoint, it translates the request into binary FastCGI frames and forwards it over the socket to an idle PHP-FPM worker.
  4. Execution and Cleanup: The worker executes the script, streams the generated HTML or JSON back to Nginx, runs its memory cleanup routines, and marks itself ready for the next request.

Fault Tolerance by Design

The real beauty of PHP-FPM is its fault isolation.

In a long-lived Node.js or Python process, if a native C extension crashes with a segmentation fault, the entire server process dies instantly. All ongoing requests for every user are abruptly dropped.

In PHP-FPM, if Worker 4104 encounters a fatal segmentation fault or exceeds its memory limit, only that single worker terminates.

The master process detects the signal, logs the crash, and spawns a brand new worker in fractions of a millisecond. None of the other workers are affected, and no other users experience downtime.

PHP 8's Tracing JIT: Compiling Bytecode to Native Silicon

With PHP 8, the language took its biggest evolutionary leap since PHP 7: the introduction of a Just-In-Time (JIT) Compiler.

In standard execution, the Zend VM is an interpreter. It runs an infinite loop in C that fetches an opcode, looks up the opcode handler in a table, and executes it:

while (1) {
    execute(opline++);
}

While this interpreter loop is heavily optimized, it still incurs CPU overhead: jumping through handler tables and maintaining VM stack frames.

The PHP 8 JIT bypasses this interpreter loop for performance-critical code.

PHP 8 implements a Tracing JIT:

  1. Profile Recording: As the Zend VM executes opcodes, the JIT monitors frequently executed code paths (known as hot loops or hot traces).
  2. Intermediate Representation: When an opcode sequence exceeds a designated execution threshold, the JIT records the exact type profile of the variables involved.
  3. Native Assembly Generation: Using DynASM (the assembler library originally created for LuaJIT), the JIT translates those opcodes directly into raw machine instructions: x86-64 or ARM64 assembly.
  4. Direct Execution: On subsequent iterations, the CPU executes the machine code directly on physical hardware, completely bypassing the Zend VM interpreter loop.

For typical I/O-bound web applications waiting on database queries, the JIT provides modest gains (around 5% to 15%), because database latency dominates execution time.

However, for CPU-bound tasks like image manipulation, mathematical modeling, JSON parsing, and machine learning inference, the JIT allows PHP to run at speeds approaching native C.

The Paradigm Shift: Why the Architecture Won

PHP's reputation as a "messy" language was earned in the late 1990s when developers mixed raw SQL directly into HTML templates.

Yet while developer trends have cycled through countless runtimes, frameworks, and deployment paradigms, PHP has quietly remained the workhorse of the internet.

Why? Because its core architectural philosophy was right all along:

  1. Shared-Nothing means bulletproof reliability. No memory leaks across requests, no cross-user state pollution, and instant crash isolation.
  2. OPcache delivers compiled-language speed. Source files are compiled once into shared memory, eliminating disk I/O and parsing overhead.
  3. The 16-byte zval maximizes cache locality. Small primitives never touch the heap, keeping CPU caches full and latency low.
  4. Copy-on-Write provides safety without waste. You get clean pass-by-value semantics without duplicating memory blocks.
  5. PHP-FPM scales effortlessly. Pre-forked worker pools map cleanly to multi-core servers without complex multi-threading bugs.

PHP does not survive despite its execution model. It thrives because of it.

By accepting that every request is an ephemeral, isolated event, PHP achieved what long-lived runtimes still struggle to guarantee: effortless scalability, rock-solid stability, and a developer experience where you never have to restart the server to see your code run.

When you look at modern PHP through the lens of the Zend Engine, what was the biggest revelation that changed your perspective on how the language actually works? And how do you see the balance between shared-nothing runtimes and persistent app servers evolving?

References:

  • PHP Internals Handbook: The Zend Engine & zval Architecture
  • PHP Official Documentation: OPcache & Preloading Configuration
  • Dmitry Stogov: phpng Architectural Proposal and Implementation
  • PHP RFC: JIT Compilation in PHP 8
  • Nikita Popov: Internal Memory Management in PHP 7 and 8

articles.description: I bought an old GraLab darkroom timer: a big analog dial built for timing photo prints under a red...
articles.body_html:
I bought an old GraLab darkroom timer: a big analog dial built for timing photo prints under a red safelight. The first time I turned that knob I thought: this is a safe dial.

The plan is to gut it into a game controller (encoder behind the dial, a Pico inside, the toggle as a button). But before soldering anything, I wanted to know if the game was actually fun. So I built it for the web first.

🔐 Play it: haugf.com/vault. A new vault every night at midnight.

The game in 10 seconds

  • 3 tumblers, 60 seconds. Turn slowly and feel for the thunk: one click heavier than the rest, plus a buzz on your phone. Then lock it in.
  • The guard. You hear footsteps, the door opens, and you freeze. Move while he's looking and you're spotted (−10s). Three strikes and you're busted.
  • Daily, like Wordle. Everyone gets the same vault. Your first run is the official one, and after that it's practice.

Design before code

My one rule: mock it first, then build it. The times I jumped straight to code were the times I redid work.

  • One phone screen, no scrolling. LOCK sits in the thumb zone.
  • Stay in the darkroom. Black, safelight red. Run out of time and your print burns.
  • Make it shareable. Wordle's grid is why people post it, so this has one: 
🫆 Darkroom Heist #1
💰 38.2s · Safecracker
🟥🟥🟩
🟩
💰
haugf.com/vault

🟩 crack · 🟥 bad lock · 🔦 spotted · 💰 the final crack

How it's built

One HTML file. No framework, no build step.

Piece How
Daily vault Date-seeded RNG, so everyone gets the same vault and there's no server
Dial <canvas> with touch drag, mouse wheel and arrow keys
Sound All synthesized with Web Audio, no audio files
Haptics navigator.vibrate
Hosting S3 + CloudFront

iOS gotcha: the sound didn't start until your first LOCK press, because iOS only unlocks Web Audio after a tap. The fix is to unlock it on any touch with a silent buffer.

Launching it at a hackathon

I was coaching MakeCU (Columbia's hackathon) and told the room to play for a shirt. CloudFront logs from the first weekend:

  • 57 visitors, 86 game loads
  • 40 of 57 on iPhone
  • 48 came from links tapped in group chats
  • Sunday, with no hackathon push: 26 new players

What playtesters told me:

  • Too much scrolling. → the one-screen layout
  • Text highlights while dragging. → turned off selection everywhere but the share text
  • Caught while holding still. → still open: lifting your finger should count as frozen
  • Make the right number more obvious. → Easy and Hard modes are in mockups

A global leaderboard: Today's Crew


Sample board for illustration.

The backend is tiny: one Python Lambda behind a function URL, plus one DynamoDB table keyed by vault and device. It costs pennies.

  • Never block sharing. You always see your result first. You go on the board under three random letters, and you can tap your row any day to sign your real initials.
  • No bad words in three letters. There's a blocklist, checked in the game and on the server. Try one and you get an Easter egg: muzzle flash, gunshot, BANG., and your letters get shot out.

What's next

  • Fair freezing
  • Easy / Hard modes
  • Real art by Ally
  • The actual GraLab controller, on a screen at Wonderville

New vault every night. Come crack it: haugf.com/vault

articles.body_html:
An agent is not just a chat window with better manners.

It can call a model five times, search an internal system, open a ticket, write to a database, and hand a task to another agent before anyone notices the token count climbing.

That is useful. It also means the hardest question is no longer “which model should we use?”

It is:

What is this agent allowed to reach, spend, and change?

An agent gateway is the layer that answers that question in one place.

It sits between agents and the things they call: model providers, MCP tools, internal APIs, and sometimes other agents. It can authenticate the caller, decide whether a request is allowed, route it, limit cost, and leave a trail for the person who has to explain what happened later.

Without it, every agent tends to bring its own API keys, its own logging, its own routing logic, and its own interpretation of “just call the tool.”

That is fine for a prototype. It gets awkward very quickly in production.

First, what problem is an agent gateway solving?

Agents create three different traffic paths:

  1. Agent to model

    The normal LLM request. This is where model choice, rate limits, fallbacks, and token cost matter.

  2. Agent to tool

    Usually MCP traffic, but also direct HTTP APIs, databases, queues, or internal services. This is where the agent can read or change something real.

  3. Agent to agent

    One agent delegates work to another. This is often called A2A traffic.

A normal LLM gateway usually handles the first path well. It routes requests, tracks tokens, chooses fallbacks, and can apply prompt controls.

An MCP gateway handles the second path. It decides which tools an agent can discover and invoke, and it may handle the credentials used upstream.

An agent gateway tries to govern all of those paths with one policy model.

That distinction matters because model calls are mostly about what the agent says. Tool calls are about what the agent does.

The gateway is not the agent brain

This gets confused a lot.

The agent framework decides how to plan, reason, retry, and call tools. The gateway does not replace that.

The gateway is closer to a bouncer with a ledger:

  • Who is this agent?
  • Which model can it use?
  • Which tools can it call?
  • Can it use the production version of that tool?
  • Can it spend another $50 on a loop?
  • Should this request require approval?
  • What happened before and after the tool ran?

If you have ever put an API gateway in front of services, the idea is familiar. The difference is that the caller is now a system that may create more calls on its own.

Why model routing alone stops being enough

Model routing is useful. It can choose a cheaper model for simple work, switch providers during an outage, and stop one team from consuming every available request.

But model routing does not answer this:

Can the support agent issue a refund?
Can the coding agent run a production migration?
Can the research agent read a customer export?
Can the finance agent call the payroll tool?

Those are tool-boundary questions.

The most dangerous agent behavior usually starts after the model has finished generating text. The model suggests a tool call. Then a credential reaches a real system. The tool returns data or changes state. The agent sees the result and decides what to do next.

That is the path a serious gateway needs to control.

What a production agent gateway should actually do

There are six things worth evaluating in any agent gateway. Everything else is detail until these are clear.

Control The question to ask Why it matters
Protocol coverage Does it govern LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic? Agents can use all three in one task.
Identity Can it identify the agent and the human or service behind it? One shared master key is not governance.
Tool policy Can it allow, deny, scope, and inspect tool calls? Tools read and change real systems.
Spend limits Can it stop a loop at a hard budget? Reporting cost after the loop finishes is not a limit.
Observability Can you trace the complete chain across model and tool calls? Incidents rarely stay inside one request.
Deployment Can it run where your data and credentials are allowed to be? Security rules often decide this before features do.

The two questions that separate a real evaluation from a feature checklist are:

Can it block a risky tool call before execution?

Can it stop an agent from spending more after a budget is reached?

If the answer to either is “we can see it in the dashboard later,” that is observability, not control.

Seven agent gateways worth putting on a shortlist

The list below is not a universal ranking. “Best” depends on where you run, which protocols you need, and whether you want a managed service or a platform your team owns.

Product capabilities change quickly in this category. Treat this as a shortlist of agent gateways for a proof of concept, then verify the current documentation, licensing, and operational requirements before a long-term decision.

1. Bifrost

Best fit: Teams that want one self-hosted gateway governing LLM, MCP, and agent-to-agent (A2A) traffic, especially where VPC, on-prem, or air-gapped deployment matters.

Bifrost combines model routing and MCP access behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Its published governance model centers on virtual keys, which can scope models, providers, tools, budgets, and rate limits per agent, team, or customer.

The useful part is not the provider count. It is being able to give a coding agent one identity with a limited tool bundle and a hard budget, instead of handing it a general-purpose key that works everywhere.

Its published MCP features include curated virtual MCP tool bundles, layered tool filtering, upstream OAuth support, and deployments inside a customer VPC or on-premises environment. Teams evaluating latency-sensitive workloads can also review its published benchmark methodology and results.

For agent-to-agent traffic, Bifrost has a documented Agent Gateway with A2A support. You register an existing agent from its agent card, control which callers can reach it, forward credentials, handle push callbacks, and inspect each run in Agent Logs. That puts LLM, MCP, and agent-to-agent traffic behind one gateway.

Ask during evaluation: Can the same policy identity govern the model request, the MCP tool call, and the A2A agent call?

2. Kong AI Gateway

Best fit: Organizations already running Kong Gateway or Kong Konnect for API management.

Kong AI Gateway is compelling when the infrastructure team already trusts Kong with normal API traffic. Instead of introducing a separate AI control plane, the team can extend the existing one to LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic.

Kong publishes central authentication, authorization, rate limiting, token quotas, audit trails, model routing, prompt controls, and MCP server generation on top of managed APIs.

The tradeoff is obvious too. If you do not already use Kong, adopting a broad API management platform only for agent traffic may be more platform than you need.

Ask during evaluation: Are tool-level controls as mature as model-side controls for the exact MCP flows you run?

3. LiteLLM

Best fit: Teams that want an open source, self-hosted Python proxy covering LLM routing, MCP tools, and A2A agents.

LiteLLM started as a way to call many model providers through one interface, and its proxy now includes an MCP gateway and an Agent Gateway for A2A agents. It is MIT licensed and runs in your own environment.

On the A2A side, you register agents in the admin UI or in config.yaml, and the proxy serves each agent's card and forwards calls. Access is checked per virtual key and team, and the logs show who called which agent along with latency and cost. Its docs also cover per-agent iteration budgets and a kill switch. A2A agents can sit behind the proxy next to model and MCP traffic, which keeps the setup in one place.

It is a Python service you operate yourself, so plan for the database, upgrades, and scaling. Some governance features, such as SSO and audit logs, are listed under its enterprise offering, so check what the open source tier covers for your requirements.

Ask during evaluation: Can your team own the proxy, its database, and its upgrade path, and which governance features does your tier include?

4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway

Best fit: AWS-native teams that want a fully managed gateway and are comfortable keeping the control plane inside AWS.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway can turn APIs, Lambda functions, and existing services into MCP-compatible tools. It supports inbound identity checks, outbound credential injection, OAuth flows, tool search, model routing, and passthrough targets for agent-to-agent traffic.

This is the quickest route for a team already building on Bedrock and AWS identity. There is less gateway infrastructure to run and fewer components to assemble.

The limit is also clear. It is a managed AWS service. If you need on-prem deployment, a multi-cloud control plane, or an air-gapped environment, this is probably not the right baseline.

Ask during evaluation: Which credentials remain AWS-managed, and which identities can be passed through to downstream tools?

5. IBM ContextForge

Best fit: Teams that need to federate a messy real-world collection of MCP servers, REST APIs, gRPC services, and agents.

IBM ContextForge is more about discovery and federation than it is about being only a model router. It can put multiple internal services behind one endpoint, translate REST or gRPC services into tool-friendly forms, and connect external agents through A2A.

That makes it interesting when the core problem is not “which model do I route to?” but “how do I give agents a safe catalog of twenty years of internal APIs?”

Its published capabilities include user-scoped OAuth, retries, rate limits, OpenTelemetry, an admin UI, and air-gapped deployment support.

Ask during evaluation: Do you need per-agent hard budget enforcement, or is tool and service federation the primary problem?

6. Agent Router

Best fit: Teams already committed to Envoy, Kubernetes Gateway API, and a platform-owned data plane.

Agent Router is the project previously known as Envoy AI Gateway. It is built as an additive agent and model layer around Envoy Gateway.

It publishes model-provider routing, token-aware quotas, MCP multiplexing, tool filtering, OAuth with PKCE, CEL-based authorization, and OpenTelemetry metrics and traces. It also has a local mode for trying the gateway without a full Kubernetes environment.

The project is a strong fit for teams that want an Envoy-shaped control plane. The open-source path leaves several platform concerns to you, including operational UI, SSO, RBAC, and some guardrail choices.

Ask during evaluation: Are you buying an Envoy foundation or trying to avoid building one?

7. Azure API Management

Best fit: Teams already running Azure API Management, or building on Azure, that want AI traffic governed as part of a larger managed API platform.

Microsoft's AI gateway is not a separate product. It is a set of capabilities on Azure API Management, so the policies, monitoring, and developer portal your API team already uses extend to AI traffic.

For models, it offers an LLM token limit policy (tokens per minute or periodic quotas, keyed by subscription, IP, or a custom expression), backend load balancing, and circuit breakers. For tools, it can expose a REST API or an existing server as an MCP server, with policies for rate limits, JWT validation, and IP filtering. For agents, it can import A2A agent APIs, expose the agent card through the gateway, and apply policies to the traffic. Monitoring runs through Azure Monitor and Application Insights.

Check the details against your plan. Microsoft's docs label the unified model API and the AI gateway integration in Microsoft Foundry as preview. The MCP and A2A pages I reviewed carry no preview label, but they list limits: MCP support covers tools but not resources or prompts, MCP policies currently apply to all tools on a server, and A2A import supports JSON-RPC agents only. Some newer AI gateway features arrive first through an early release channel on classic tiers.

Ask during evaluation: Which of the features you need are generally available on your API Management tier today, and which are still in preview?

The shortcut comparison

If you need... Start with...
One self-hosted gateway for LLM, MCP, and A2A traffic with VPC or on-prem options Bifrost
Existing Kong operations and broad API governance Kong AI Gateway
An open source, self-hosted Python proxy for LLM, MCP, and A2A LiteLLM
Fully managed AWS integration Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Federation of MCP, REST, gRPC, and agent services IBM ContextForge
Envoy and Kubernetes Gateway API as the data plane Agent Router
A managed gateway inside an Azure and API Management footprint Azure API Management

That is a starting point, not a purchase decision.

The tool boundary is the real test

Every vendor can show you a routing demo.

The better test is a tool call that should be denied.

For example:

Agent: “Delete the inactive customer records.”
Tool request: DELETE /customers?status=inactive
Policy: this agent may read customer data, but may not delete it.
Expected result: tool execution never happens.

Now make it harder:

Agent: “Issue a refund under $50.”
Tool request: refund(customer_id, amount)
Policy: agent may refund up to $50 only for the current user’s account.
Expected result: identity, amount, ownership, and tool argument rules all pass before execution.

Then test the return path:

Tool result: contains an access token or another customer's data.
Expected result: the result is blocked or redacted before the model sees it.

That last part gets missed. A tool can be allowed to run and still return something the model should not receive.

You want controls before execution and controls after execution.

An agent gateway evaluation that will not waste three weeks

Do not start with a vendor demo. Start with three real agent journeys from your environment.

Journey 1: the normal safe path

An agent reads an internal document, summarizes it with an approved model, and opens a draft ticket. This proves ordinary routing, identity, audit, and policy work.

Journey 2: the request that must stop

An agent tries a tool call outside its scope. This proves the gateway can prevent execution rather than simply report it.

Journey 3: the runaway loop

An agent is intentionally given a task that retries, switches models, and makes repeated tool calls. This proves budgets and rate limits are enforced before the invoice arrives.

For every journey, ask for four pieces of evidence:

  1. The caller identity
  2. The policy decision
  3. The upstream request and result, with sensitive data redacted
  4. The trace that connects the model call, tool call, and final agent output

If a product cannot make that evidence easy to collect, incident response will be unpleasant later.

The questions people forget to ask

Can it use the end user’s identity?

An agent acting as the user should not quietly become a service account with broader access. Check whether the gateway can exchange, forward, or scope identity per user and per tool.

Can it kill access instantly?

If a tool server is compromised or an agent starts behaving badly, can you disable one agent key or tool bundle immediately without redeploying every agent?

Are budgets hard limits?

Cost dashboards are useful. A budget that only alerts after a request succeeds is not a budget. Test whether the next request is rejected once the limit is reached.

What happens during provider failure?

Fallbacks can improve reliability. They can also accidentally send a sensitive prompt to a provider you did not approve. Make provider fallback policy explicit.

Does it only cover the happy transport?

MCP has multiple transports. Tools may use HTTP, SSE, streamable HTTP, or stdio. Ask which path gets the same identity, policy, audit, and guardrail coverage.

The honest conclusion

An agent gateway is not a magic layer that makes autonomous systems safe.

It is the place where you can finally make the rules visible and enforceable.

The right agent gateway is usually not the one with the longest provider list. It is the one that can live where you need it to live, intercept the traffic you actually have, stop the tool call you are afraid of, and leave enough evidence behind for someone else to understand the decision.

Start with your risky tool call. Everything else gets clearer after that.

  • LiteLLM MCP Gateway documentation
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway documentation

  • Agent Router project

articles.title: How to make Vue Dynamic Components more stable
articles.description: Hey Folks, it's me again!  Today, I would like to share with you how I recently made the Vue Dynamic...
articles.body_html:
Hey Folks, it's me again!

Today, I would like to share with you how I recently made the Vue Dynamic Components bit more stable to avoid unexpected cases, improve props stability, and in general provide better developer experience.

This is how I solved my problem, if you encounter the same and you solved it differently, please let me know in the comments! :)

Problem

The default Vue Dynamic Components definitely gives you a lot of flexibility but to my taste a bit too much - especially if you want to have a better Type Safety with TypeScript. Let's take a look at the following example:

<script>
import { ref } from 'vue';
import AwesomeButton from './AwesomeButton.vue';

const shouldDisplayButton = ref(true);
</script>

<template>
  <div>
    <component
      :is="shouldDisplayButton ? 'AsewomeButton' : 'div'"
      @click="console.log('Hello World')"
      :text="Click me"
    ></component>
  </div>
</template>

There are two problems here:

  1. The prop is accepts either a string or an actual Vue component - which makes it easy have unexpected and sometimes difficult to track bugs (in the example, I made a typo 'AsewomeButton' instead of 'AwesomeButton'
  2. There is no typechecking for the props that are passed to this dynamic component which can result in a div receiving text and @click handler.

These problems can be difficult to track as the linter, compiler or TS check could miss them as technically they are correct.

Solution

We first tried with the Eslint rule that would forbid having a regular string in :is but this didn't solve our problem of props so we decided to create our wrapper abstraction over native Vue <component :is> that looks more or less like following:

import { h } from 'vue'
import type { Component, NativeElements, SetupContext, VNode } from 'vue'

type NativeTag = keyof NativeElements

type ComponentProps<C> = C extends new (...args: never[]) => {
  $props: infer P
}
  ? Omit<NonNullable<P>, 'is'>
  : C extends (props: infer P, ...args: never[]) => unknown
    ? Omit<P, 'is'>
    : Record<string, unknown>

type DynamicProps<C> = C extends NativeTag
  ? NativeElements[C]
  : ComponentProps<C>

// The `Component` type says nothing about props, so none could be checked.
type SpecificComponent<T> = Component extends T
  ? 'Type `is` as a specific component, not as `Component`'
  : unknown

export type DynamicComponentProps<T extends NativeTag | Component> = {
  is: T & SpecificComponent<T>
} & DynamicProps<T>

export function DynamicComponent<T extends NativeTag | Component>(
  props: DynamicComponentProps<T>,
  { slots }: Pick<SetupContext, 'slots'>,
): VNode {
  const { is, ...rest } = props
  return h(is, rest, slots)
}

DynamicComponent.inheritAttrs = false

There is a bunch of code so let me explain below what most important parts of it does:

NativeTag

There might be cases where the ternary would result in native HTML tag and that we don't want to forbid. So scenario like :is="'div'" should still be allowed.

ComponentProps & DynamicProps

We want to typecheck the passed component and dynamic props as a union of ternary elements. So if we expect that this dynamic component can be either X or Y, the only possible passable props should be the ones that are common for both X & Y.

SpecificComponent

What shouldn't be allowed is this: :is="'AwesomeComponent'"(passed as a string). This though should be possible :is="AwesomeComponent"

DynamicComponent

We use the Vue render function to render this component. For the users, the usage will be almost the same as the native Vue dynamic component - the only thing we replace is <component> with `' (to avoid name collisions).

Summary

This helped us discovered few cases that were working but were really error prone (a typo would break the page/component). We also have a rule that disalows usage of :is that results to string that is not native html tag, and also prompts the developer to use DynamicComponent instead. This way we advocate this more safer and stable solution to other devs.

Let me know how you are solving similar problems! :)

articles.title: Designing Fault-Tolerant API Through Idempotency
articles.description: So imagine I’m reading your post. I click Like, the heart turns red, and the request times out. My...
articles.body_html:
So imagine I’m reading your post. I click Like, the heart turns red, and the request times out. My frontend’s retry logic sends it again.

This time, the success reply arrives. The heart turns grey.
I know I liked your post. But your code apparently has other plans because its not FAULT TOLERANT.

Fault tolerance is an application’s ability to keep working correctly when part of the system fails. Retrying can help us recover from a temporary connection failure, but our API has to handle the second attempt safely.

For database writes, there’s a catch. Saving the change and delivering the HTTP response are separate steps. The connection can drop after the database commits, leaving the client unsure whether the write succeeded.

Let’s follow that click through MongoDB and PostgreSQL on Neon, then make the retry safe in both.

One click became two requests

Our endpoint is POST /posts/42/toggle-like. It reverses the current state. If my like exists, remove it. Otherwise, create it.

Here’s how one click manages to do both.

  1. The API saves my like.
  2. The connection drops before the success reply reaches my browser.
  3. The browser retries.
  4. The API finds the like and removes it. This reply arrives successfully.

The first write succeeded. Only its reply was lost.

The retry recovered from the connection failure, but it also reversed the user’s action. Making this endpoint fault tolerant means handling both parts correctly.

Our like can live in a MongoDB document or a PostgreSQL row on Neon. Either database will execute a fresh request to remove it. Our API told it to toggle, and it followed the instruction.

Could we wrap the toggle in a transaction?

Yes. A transaction groups database changes so they all commit together or all roll back. That’s atomicity. MongoDB supports transactions across documents on replica sets and sharded clusters. Neon supports PostgreSQL transactions. MongoDB transactions · PostgreSQL transactions

In our example, though, the first transaction already committed before the reply disappeared. The retry starts a new transaction and reverses the like.

Both transactions succeed. I’ve now unliked your post with excellent data integrity.

A row lock also ends when its transaction finishes, leaving the later retry free to make another change. PostgreSQL row locks

We need to change what repeating the request does.

Make the request say what I mean

Instead of asking the API to toggle, ask it to make sure my like exists.

The first request creates it. The retry finds it and leaves it there.

That’s idempotency; repeating the request has the same intended effect as sending it once. The responses can differ while the intended effect stays the same.

We can use PUT /posts/42/like to ensure the like exists. For an unlike, DELETE /posts/42/like ensures the like is absent.

The handler’s database operation must implement that promise. Changing the HTTP verb alone leaves the original toggle behaviour in place.

MongoDB can create a missing like with an upsert. PostgreSQL on Neon can use INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Both need a unique rule for the user-and-post pair so simultaneous requests also produce one like.

Implementation examples

MongoDB

Create the unique index once. Then use the upsert in the request handler, taking userId from the signed-in session.

// One-time setup
await likes.createIndex(
  { postId: 1, userId: 1 },
  { unique: true }
);

// In the PUT handler
await likes.updateOne(
  { postId, userId },
  { $setOnInsert: { likedAt: new Date() } },
  { upsert: true }
);

An existing like keeps its original timestamp.

PostgreSQL on Neon

Give the likes table a primary key on (post_id, user_id), then run this parameterised query.

INSERT INTO likes (post_id, user_id)
VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, user_id) DO NOTHING;

The retry finds the existing pair and leaves it alone.

If you keep a separate like counter, increase it only when a new like was inserted, in the same transaction.

What if I need to keep the toggle endpoint?

The PUT approach above repeats the same desired state. If we keep POST /posts/42/toggle-like, we need a way to recognise that a particular action already happened.

Give each deliberate click an idempotency key. This key identifies one action across all its retries. The client reuses it when retrying and generates a new key for a new deliberate click.

In one transaction, claim the key under a unique constraint scoped to the user and endpoint, apply the toggle, and save its result. When the same key comes back, return the saved result.

Now test the exact failure. Let the write succeed, drop its HTTP reply, and retry. There should still be one like when you refresh.

Whether the like lives in MongoDB or Neon, both attempts now leave us with the result we wanted. One click. One like.

So if I liked your post. The heart should stay red 😂.
I hope this helps you and can guide in making your code

Thanks for reading 👍

articles.title: Car hacking through identity servers: what the research proves
articles.description: Car hacking research by Shah and Curry shows how identity administration became app authority, with permissioned US tests and a reported earlier fix.
articles.body_html:
Car hacking research published by Shubham Shah and Sam Curry shows how administrative access to an identity service can become authority over a physical vehicle. The familiar systems are customer records, sign-in sessions and the mobile app's credentials. A car is where the consequences become unusually tangible. Their account gives developers a reason to inspect the services that define the owner their application trusts.

TL;DR

  • Both primary writeups appeared on November 7, describing earlier research. Publication and discovery have different dates.
  • Curry's US companion reports same-day remediation after disclosure and limits complete account-to-vehicle testing to US accounts and vehicles.
  • Shah's Australian July account has a separate scope and leaves its current remediation status unspecified.
  • The researchers report owner-equivalent app authority and permissioned physical demonstrations. Model, subscription and active-service conditions still matter.
  • The defensive review starts with administrative identity access and ends with a check of what actually happened at the physical endpoint.

Car hacking starts with trusted identity

A connected-car app relies on online services to associate a customer with a garage of vehicles and the commands those vehicles support. Once the customer completes sign-in, the app obtains the credentials its services expect. The service then acts on the account-to-vehicle relationship.

Shah and Curry's US companion describes access to production identity systems handling customer logins for two unnamed automakers. From those systems, the researchers could create valid sessions for customer accounts managed by the affected deployments. For accounts with active connected services, they report the same remote access available through the owner's app.

That relationship explains the developer consequence. A downstream service can correctly validate the credentials presented to it while the upstream identity defining the customer has already been rewritten. Reviewing token acceptance alone leaves the question of who can change the trusted account facts.

For a defensive review, I would draw the authority boundaries before drawing the feature flow. Which system can change the customer record? Which system completes sign-in? Which credentials does the vehicle service accept? Those questions make the role of each component visible without turning the article into an operational exploit walkthrough.

The distinction travels beyond cars. Any application whose permissions depend on an upstream customer record needs to understand who can change that record. The recommendation comes from the reported mechanism; we have not measured how often other products share it.

Read publication, disclosure and test scope separately

The current news event is the publication of the research. Both primary pages show November 7. Curry dates discovery and disclosure to early 2026. Shah's Australian account describes collaboration beginning in July.

These are separate source timelines. A single chronological story that moves from July discovery to an early-year fix would invent a relationship the sources do not establish. Keeping the two accounts attributed is clearer than trying to repair their chronology with assumptions.

Source account Reported research scope Reported remediation
Shah's Australian writeup One unnamed automaker across two brands; research beginning in July; owned or permissioned vehicles No matching remediation timeline supplied; current Australian status unspecified
Shah and Curry's US companion Two unnamed automakers' affected identity directories across multiple regions; complete vehicle-chain testing only in the US Both automakers reportedly remediated the reported vulnerability approximately two hours after receiving the early-2026 disclosure and rotated affected credentials

Shah's final paragraph claims broader combined command reach in Australia, the United States and Canada. Curry's explicit physical-test limit remains narrower. Directory reach, a claimed capability and a completed physical demonstration are different evidence categories.

We therefore have no basis to identify the redacted manufacturers, call every model vulnerable, describe Canada as a complete-chain physical test, or announce a new worldwide unpatched emergency. The Australian status left unspecified also gives us no basis to say that it remains open.

Administration needs its own review

In the Australian account, Shah describes management interfaces that relied on keys delivered in browser JavaScript. He also reports administrator credentials in a vendor bundle that worked in production. A browser-delivered bundle is an effective way to distribute bytes widely, which is an awkward property for something intended to stay secret.

The US companion describes a different part of the boundary. The edge treated a request path as static content while the identity backend reached an administration console. Security depended on those interpretations agreeing. The administration tooling ultimately allowed code to run inside the identity service and reach customer records behind the public filtering boundary.

This article deliberately leaves out request payloads, encoded paths, credential values, executable commands and the complete operational chain. The explanatory point is the mismatch between layers and the authority of the process behind the edge.

The independently read PingIDM 7.2 production-hardening guide tells operators to remove or protect development and debug tools before production. It also states that authentication for the console is separate from authentication for IDM.

That separate login is easy to miss if a review begins and ends with the consumer authentication journey. An administrative surface can have its own credentials, configuration and exposure. The inventory has to include that surface explicitly. This is versioned documentation, marked no longer maintained; it is useful evidence of the documented hardening boundary, rather than a new vendor response.

A session and an app token have different jobs

The word token can obscure important distinctions. Administrator access controls identity records. A customer session represents a completed sign-in. The mobile app obtains tokens accepted by the services it calls afterward. The researchers' account follows those boundaries until the connected service accepts owner-equivalent access.

The US multi-factor finding also depends on the integrity of the upstream records. The source describes administrative control affecting the login information and the destination for email verification. Completing that journey verified control over the rewritten account facts.

Shah describes a separate Australian authentication misconfiguration that allowed his chain to skip the extra factor. These findings need their regional configuration context. Declaring multi-factor authentication universally broken would discard the detail that makes the report useful.

Keep the extra factor, and review the systems allowed to define its owner and verification route. A defensive account-recovery review should ask which authority can change a contact destination and what other services will trust that change. That is a review question, not an assertion that every recovery flow is vulnerable.

It is also worth naming each credential in the design review by its job. A diagram labelled administrator access, customer session and app authority is easier to reason about than three boxes carrying the same generic token label.

Physical confirmation changed the strength of the evidence

The most useful detail arrives in the US companion's vehicle-command section. The authors explicitly say that an accepted API command did not prove that the car had acted on it. They refreshed vehicle status and confirmed the physical result with the owner beside the vehicle. Shah unlocked and started it, then stopped the engine and locked it again.

That observation takes the report beyond a successful response on a laptop. It also preserves the permission boundary: these were vehicles the researchers owned or were allowed to interact with. We performed no automotive testing for the episode or this article.

The supported capability matters as much as the confirmation method. Curry describes model and subscription dependencies, and accounts with active connected services. Door unlock and remote engine start are among the reported app commands. Neither primary establishes that the chain defeated an immobilizer or allowed someone to drive away.

For a system with physical effects, I would write the outcome test separately from the API test. What response did the service accept? What state did the service subsequently report? What happened at the device itself? This report answered the physical question with an owner-side check. The article does not extend that result to an untested fleet.

A practical defensive review

Start by inventorying the administrative surfaces that can change trusted customer identity. Give each retained console an explicit owner and identify the authentication system protecting it. Remove unused development tools and protect the tools that remain, consistent with the versioned production guidance.

Then review the boundary between edge filtering and backend interpretation. The source describes a case in which those layers disagreed about the request they were handling. A rule at the edge needs to be evaluated alongside the backend's actual interpretation, rather than treated as the final authority simply because it blocked the expected route.

Finally, follow the trusted account facts downstream. List which services consume ownership, contact destinations and completed sign-in state. Identify which upstream authorities can change them. A useful review should leave the team able to explain who can redefine the owner that each service believes.

The defensive reading focuses on protecting the service's authority. The HN discussion includes practical reasons people like remote features, including checking a forgotten lock and warming or cooling a car. Convenience creates a real service responsibility. Customers can reasonably want the feature and expect its authority to be protected.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I would audit administrative paths into customer identity before trusting them with physical controls. The reported US remediation deserves credit. The publication makes the authority boundary worth reviewing without establishing a current worldwide emergency.

FAQ

Was this discovered on November 7?

That is the publication date on the two primary pages. Curry dates his discovery and disclosure to early 2026. Shah describes Australian research beginning in July. The sources do not supply one reconciled joint timeline.

Were every region and every vehicle physically tested?

Curry explicitly limits complete account-to-vehicle testing to US accounts and vehicles. Shah describes Australian permissioned testing and a broader combined capability claim. The sources do not establish complete physical testing in every region or across every model and subscription.

Does remote engine start prove that someone can drive away?

The primary writeups establish supported app commands and the stated permissioned physical demonstrations. Driving away and immobilizer defeat are not established by those results.

What should developers take from the identity mechanism?

Review who can change the trusted customer record and which downstream services consume it. A valid session can rest on a rewritten upstream identity, so administrative access deserves an explicit place in the authorization review.

Sources

  • Shubham Shah — Australian connected-car account
  • Shubham Shah and Sam Curry — US companion, scope and disclosure timeline
  • Ping Identity — PingIDM 7.2 production hardening
  • Hacker News — connected-feature discussion
  • Cover portrait: Magistr8, Wikimedia Commons, CC0; cropped, background-masked and resized without generated detail. Sam Curry's official About page corroborates identity. Photograph date unspecified; no endorsement or current-reaction claim. No film/GIF or anime meme is reproduced in this written edition.

Video media credits

The accompanying video uses a ScreenJunkies/GIPHY Jurassic Park caricature, whose native source links to ScreenJunkies, and the Imgflip Pigeon template. Each is a silent excerpt or still of at most two seconds, transformed as fictional process commentary. Neither depicts an actual automaker reaction. Hosting and publisher provenance grant no blanket reuse licence or legal clearance. These assets are not reproduced in this written edition.
