articles.title: I shipped an app to the Microsoft Store. It has no code.
articles.description: We got Publora into the Microsoft Store. I expected this to involve building a Windows app. Instead,...
articles.body_html:
We got Publora into the Microsoft Store. I expected this to involve building a Windows app. Instead, we ended up submitting something that contains almost nothing except pictures and instructions to open our website.

I should mention that I don't write the code myself. Claude does. I usually handle the questions, the testing and the occasional argument about whether something is actually finished. This time there wasn't much code for either of us to worry about.

I unpacked the .msix package we were submitting and looked through its contents. Eighty-four files. Eighty of them PNGs, accounting for almost all of the package size. The remaining four were the manifest and some XML files. No .exe, no .dll, no .js.

The manifest tells Windows to launch our PWA through Edge:

--app-id=fjgokhecjlkghhifolnkkipaippljcnm
--app-fallback-url=https://app.publora.com/
--display-mode=standalone --windows-store-app

PWABuilder generated the package. What users install is essentially a standalone window for the Publora website, without the browser's usual address bar. We didn't need to write a separate Windows application.

A package with no code asked for full trust

When we uploaded the packages, both triggered a warning about runFullTrust. That's a Windows capability normally associated with desktop applications that need broader system access.

I was looking at a package containing eighty PNGs and wondering what exactly they were planning to do with all that trust.

Partner Center wanted an explanation. I used the wording from the PWABuilder guide: "Needed for PWA Hosted App model, created by pwabuilder.com." The submission passed certification.

I wouldn't treat that as a guarantee for every submission, though. The guidance we found about this warning was from 2020 and 2021, and Microsoft may handle it differently now.

The agent did everything except the last button

Claude handled most of the Partner Center process through a debug Chrome session and Playwright. Registration, identifiers, nine separate fields for the D-U-N-S number, package uploads, screenshots. There was plenty of clicking involved, and Partner Center's custom web components weren't always cooperative.

The submission itself was where Claude stopped.

The first attempt failed with a network error. On the second, Claude's safety classifier blocked the action with the message "judged this action dangerous." No further explanation.

It didn't try to get around the restriction. Instead, it got everything ready and left the final submission to me. I clicked Submit for certification, and later Publish now.

There were also the Microsoft Developer Agreement and the IARC age declaration, including the confirmation that the person accepting it is legally an adult. Those are things I needed to agree to myself.

So after Claude had worked through all the forms, I got the important job of confirming that I was old enough to use them.

The wait wasn't where they warned

Microsoft says company verification typically takes five business days. Ours took about fifteen minutes. Certification can take up to three business days; ours finished in just under two.

What took longer than expected was testing.

We needed to open the package on a real Windows machine before submitting it. Unfortunately, everyone on our team uses a Mac. We spent most of a day finding someone with Windows and then waiting for them to wake up in their time zone and try it.

The Microsoft checks were quick. Finding an awake person with Windows took longer.

curl said everything was fine

We found one problem only because we opened the app in a clean browser.

When someone visits the root of our site while signed out, the browser sends them to the landing page rather than the sign-in screen. But curl gets a 200 response from the same URL, with no HTTP redirect.

The redirect happens in the browser, so the command-line check didn't show it. We added a note for the reviewer explaining where to go if they encountered the same thing.

It's the sort of detail that's easy to miss when your tests all say the URL works.

Updates go around the store

The package is version 1.0.1, but the application itself loads from our website. When we deploy changes to Publora, those changes appear in the installed app without submitting another package to Microsoft.

That's particularly convenient for us because we're updating Publora all the time. I wouldn't want to go through store certification every time we changed something in the interface.

Our service worker already has a comment explaining why the app shell is always loaded from the network:

// the app shell (index.html / navigations) is ALWAYS served from the
// network, never from cache. A cached shell would reference old
// content-hashed chunks that a fresh deploy has already deleted (404),
// which is exactly what freezes navigation after a tab is left open
// across a deploy.

That behaviour wasn't implemented specifically for Microsoft Store. It's part of how our web app handles deployments, but it happens to be useful here too.

Why a wrapper over the website at all

Publora is now in the Microsoft Store, listed under Productivity. It's free, we didn't have to change the website, and the first submission was approved.

You could reasonably ask why we bothered when the result is essentially our website in a separate window.

Mostly because we're trying different ways for people to discover Publora. We've submitted integrations and listings to quite a few directories by now. Some bring users, some barely move the numbers, and it's difficult to predict which will be worth the effort.

This one was relatively easy to do. PWABuilder generated the package, we already had the PWA, and there was no separate Windows codebase to maintain.

I don't know yet whether the Microsoft Store will bring us any users. The listing has only been live for a day. We'll see.

I'm also curious how other people handle the final steps when working with agents. Do you let an agent submit and publish things on your behalf, or do you prefer to press those buttons yourself?

articles.title: Tauri 2: Building a Reliable Desktop App — Why the Rust Host Should Own the Lifecycle
articles.description: Tauri makes it possible to build desktop applications with web technologies: Vue for the UI and...
articles.body_html:
Tauri makes it possible to build desktop applications with web technologies: Vue for the UI and Rust for native capabilities. For a small utility, that division may be enough.

As an application grows to include background work, file operations, updates, complex startup, and unsaved editor state, a more important question appears:

Who owns the application when the WebView is hidden, reloading, unavailable, or crashed?

If the answer is still “the Vue app,” critical desktop behavior is coupled to the renderer lifecycle. A more reliable boundary is to let the Rust host own the native application lifecycle while the Vue WebView owns presentation and user interaction.

The examples below are simplified illustrations of the design, not verbatim source excerpts.

Two lifecycles, not one

A desktop application has at least two related but distinct lifecycles:

  • Native lifecycle: process startup, window creation, single-instance behavior, show/hide, tray, quit, and updater installation.
  • Renderer lifecycle: WebView loading, Vue mounting, route initialization, component teardown, and UI restoration.

A WebView reload should not mean that the application has exited. Hiding a window should not stop work that is owned by the native runtime.

A useful ownership split looks like this:

Rust host Vue WebView
Window and process lifecycle Pages, components, interaction
Single-instance and native menus Product-level state presentation
Startup deadline and native recovery UI Bootstrap UI and retry intent
Filesystem, database, secrets, process boundaries Scoped requests through typed IPC
Close/quit save barrier Collect editor leave/save decisions
Authoritative background task state Progress observation and display

The rule of thumb: if something must remain correct while the WebView is hidden or unavailable, it should not be owned exclusively by the WebView.

Start hidden; reveal only when the app is usable

Showing the main window immediately after creating it often exposes an awkward intermediate state: a blank window that could mean loading, a hang, or a failure.

A stronger startup sequence is:

  1. Rust creates the main window in a hidden state.
  2. Rust starts the startup deadline before renderer initialization.
  3. The WebView loads a small bootstrap/error shell.
  4. The renderer initializes required services and reports readiness or a recoverable error.
  5. Rust reveals the window only when the app is usable or a recoverable error can be presented. 
OS launches app
      |
Rust creates hidden main window
      |
start startup deadline
      |
WebView loads bootstrap shell
      |
initialize required services
      |
  +---+----------------------+
  |                          |
usable                  recoverable error
  |                          |
reveal window            reveal error UI

This does not mean every optional task must finish before the window appears. The important part is defining a clear usable/recoverable boundary instead of calling window.show() from an arbitrary Vue lifecycle hook.

In the project this article is based on, Rust starts the startup deadline before renderer initialization. A timeout is not a timer that blindly kills the process. It ensures that a failed startup can be presented through a native Retry/Quit dialog. Retry reloads the existing main WebView and begins a new startup generation.

That generation matters: a delayed ready event from an earlier attempt must not mark a newer attempt as ready.

A subtle Windows WebView2 deadlock

One of the more surprising desktop bugs is that a native API call can be valid but still be called from the wrong execution context.

On Windows, a synchronous Tauri command can execute inside the WebView2 IPC callback. Showing a previously hidden window directly from that synchronous callback can re-enter the message loop and deadlock the main thread. The window may stop responding, and even the startup timeout's error dialog may never appear.

The risky shape looks like this:

// Illustrative anti-pattern: do not mutate the window here.
#[tauri::command]
fn renderer_ready(window: tauri::WebviewWindow) {
    let _ = window.show();
}

A safer principle is to keep the synchronous command small: record or forward readiness, then let a lifecycle coordinator perform window mutations from the async runtime.

// Illustrative boundary, not a drop-in implementation.
#[tauri::command]
fn renderer_ready(
    state: tauri::State<'_, LifecycleState>,
) -> Result<(), String> {
    state.mark_renderer_ready()
}

// An async lifecycle coordinator observes readiness and
// performs window mutations outside the synchronous IPC callback.
async fn reveal_when_ready(/* lifecycle state, window handle */) {
    // await readiness / recoverable state
    // perform window mutation from async runtime
}

The production implementation still needs to handle duplicate readiness events, startup generations, missing window handles, and timeout races. The important architectural decision is to move the side effect out of the synchronous IPC callback.

Startup failure should be recoverable, not a blank screen

At minimum, distinguish these states:

  • starting: required initialization is still in progress.
  • ready: the application has reached its usable state.
  • recoverable_error: startup failed, but the user can see an error and retry or quit.

A successful Vue mount does not necessarily mean the application is ready. The UI may be visible while database recovery, preference loading, or a required service is still incomplete.

If retries are supported, assign a generation to each attempt. Readiness, failure, and timeout must be associated with the current generation. Otherwise, a late callback from an old WebView can overwrite the state of a newer attempt.

Closing a window is a protocol, not a method call

Shutdown becomes more interesting when the application has editors with unsaved drafts and writes that have already been admitted.

A robust leave barrier can work like this:

  1. Rust receives a close, quit, or updater-install request.
  2. Rust creates a uniquely identified request and sends it to the renderer.
  3. The renderer collects leave decisions from data owners.
  4. A user cancellation stops the transition.
  5. Owners save or preserve their drafts.
  6. Already-admitted writes are allowed to settle.
  7. The renderer acknowledges only the request it actually handled.
  8. Rust hides the window or proceeds with shutdown only after approval. 
Close / Quit request
        |
Rust creates request ID
        |
Renderer evaluates leave decisions
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
cancel     approved
   |         |
keep UI    admitted writes settle
             |
       acknowledge request
             |
       Rust hides / quits

Why use a request ID? Close requests can overlap, and the renderer can reload. A response must complete only its own pending request, not a later one.

Also keep cancellation separate from save failure. Cancellation stops the transition. A failed save should preserve the editor and show owner-level feedback; it must not be treated as a successful save.

The host needs a policy for an unresponsive renderer

If Rust waits for the renderer to make a leave decision, it cannot wait forever.

One approach is a heartbeat while the renderer is waiting for saves or user input. The host tracks the pending request and accepts only a response associated with that request. If heartbeats stop, native code handles the failure.

The project policy uses a two-second heartbeat and a fifteen-second timeout:

  • For Close, keep the window open.
  • For Quit, show a native warning about unsaved edits and let the user choose whether to keep the window open or continue quitting.

The exact numbers are product policy, not universal defaults. The invariant is more important: waiting for renderer cooperation needs a timeout, and the still-running host must own the timeout behavior.

Single-instance and platform behavior belong to the host too

Real desktop lifecycle work also includes:

  • Focusing an existing instance when the app is launched again.
  • Deciding whether close hides the window or exits the process.
  • Native Application Menu and status item behavior on macOS.
  • System tray and native caption behavior on Windows.
  • Dock/taskbar progress and notifications while the WebView is hidden.

Keeping these responsibilities in the Rust host avoids scattering platform lifecycle logic across Vue components. The frontend can still contribute commands and render state, but the host coordinates native behavior.

Trade-offs

Moving lifecycle ownership to Rust has costs:

  • You need an explicit startup state machine and request identity.
  • IPC contracts must remain narrow; not every business operation belongs in a Tauri command.
  • Host/renderer coordination must handle timeouts, reloads, and late messages.
  • Platform differences still require testing on real macOS and Windows machines.
  • Rust being closer to the OS does not mean UI state and product presentation should move into Rust.

The goal is not “put everything in Rust.” It is to give each piece of state an owner that can actually guarantee its correctness.

Takeaway

Tauri is valuable because native capabilities and web technologies can work together—not because the WebView should become the application's only control plane.

If behavior must remain correct while the window is hidden, the renderer reloads, or the WebView is unavailable, the Rust host should own or coordinate it. Vue presents state, gathers user decisions, and requests scoped capabilities through typed IPC.

That boundary gives startup, shutdown, recovery, single-instance behavior, and background work a clear authority instead of treating “the page is alive” as proof that “the application is reliable.”

Real-world implementation

These design decisions come from engineering work on Knovum, an open-source desktop application built with Tauri 2, Rust, and Vue 3.

  • Desktop foundation
  • System architecture
  • Architecture and dependency ownership
  • Knovum source code

I'd be interested in how other Tauri teams handle renderer reloads, startup coordination, and safe shutdown.

articles.title: Why am I building one more UI component lib in AI age?
articles.description: We've never had so much power to build software. You can turn an idea into a working app in a...
articles.body_html:
We've never had so much power to build software. You can turn an idea into a working app in a day/hour/minute? But there's always a catch: You AI agent can solve it too. So the question is: does anyone actually need what we/you/me're building?

I've been working in product development, open source, and startups for years, and this question has never felt more closer to home.

Every day we see more and more apps, but it's not always clear who the end user is or what problem it's going solving.

We've been working on our data grid library, RevoGrid, for quite a few years now (closer to decade if we count for Open Source part). It's an Excel-like data grid you can put into your app.

Over this time, we've built so many components and tried so many approaches that you could probably build an entire Power BI on top of it. We've spent even more time testing it and solving quests of "what to do next?"

So recently, we spent a week of our lives extracting these components into a separate UI library and making it available to everyone.

What's inside? Pretty much the building blocks we've needed for our own products: charts, AI chat interfaces, file viewers, date pickers, dropdowns, forms, time grids, timeline controls, and plenty of smaller UI components.

Basically, the stuff you need when building analytical dashboards, reporting tools, or project management apps. And it works with React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, and plain TypeScript.

We use it a lot ourselves. Pretty much all our interfaces are built with these components.

Not sure if the world needs another UI library, but here it is. It's simple, it's been tested in our own products, and maybe it'll find a place in yours too, especially if you don't want to do all the heavy lifting yourself.

Happy coding! (Or is it vibe coding now?)

articles.title: On-page GEO explains 2.8% of citation variation. Retrieval explains 32%. My null result was not a fluke
articles.description: Last week I published a calibration study showing that my tool's GEO score does not predict whether...
articles.body_html:
Last week I published a calibration study showing that my tool's GEO score does not predict whether Perplexity cites a page. The odds ratio was 0.9625, p = 0.7172. Null result, pre-registered, 341 pages.

A paper published on arxiv 10 days earlier found the same thing at a completely different scale. University of Toronto researchers Mahe Chen and Nick Koudas analyzed 158,099 ChatGPT answers and 468,037 citations across two 90-day collection windows. Their finding: on-page content properties (FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes, page speed) explain only 2.8% of citation variation within a website on ChatGPT. Retrieval, which pages the engine's own search returns for its rewritten sub-queries, explains 32%. Over 11 times more.

My null result was not a fluke. It was a small-scale confirmation of a large-scale finding.

What the Toronto paper measured

The researchers collected 158,099 ChatGPT answers across two 90-day windows, yielding 468,037 citations. They decomposed what drives a citation into three layers:

  1. Retrieval (32% of variation): which pages ChatGPT's internal search returns when it rewrites the user's query into sub-queries. Every page ChatGPT cites was first retrieved by its own search. Those sub-queries "rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results." ChatGPT writes its own queries, runs its own search, and cites from what comes back.

  2. Content properties (2.8% of variation): FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes, page speed, and other on-page signals. The things most GEO tools audit. The things my rubric checks. They explain less than 3% of why one page gets cited and another does not, within the same site.

  3. Brand recognition (significant but unquantified): the model writes brand names it already knows into its search queries, and names brands without any supporting page. Controlled experiments showed that brand names reorder rankings of products with identical facts. A brand the model knows gets cited even when the page is no better than an unknown brand's page.

Why this confirms the calibration study

My calibration study tested whether a 0-to-100 GEO score (measuring robots.txt access, schema, content structure, llms.txt, metadata, brand entity, Google AI readiness) predicts whether Perplexity cites a page. It did not. Odds ratio 0.9625, p = 0.7172.

The Toronto paper explains why. The GEO score measures on-page content properties. Those explain 2.8% of citation variation. A score that measures 2.8% of the variance cannot predict the other 97.2%. The null result was not a limitation of my sample size or my methodology. It was a correct measurement of a factor that is nearly irrelevant.

The 32% that matters, retrieval, is not something an on-page audit can measure. Retrieval depends on what ChatGPT's internal search returns for its rewritten queries. That depends on the engine's index, its query rewriting logic, and the brand recognition the model carries in its parametric memory. An audit tool that checks your page cannot see any of this.

What this means for GEO advice

The entire on-page GEO advice stack, "add FAQ schema, write answer blocks, structure your content, add llms.txt," targets the 2.8%. It is not wrong. FAQ schema and answer blocks are good practice. But they are not the lever that moves citations. The lever is retrieval: being in the pool of pages the engine's search returns for the queries it rewrites.

This is why two pages with identical on-page optimization get different citation outcomes. One is in the retrieval pool. The other is not. The on-page signals do not determine which pool you are in. The engine's search logic does.

The practical implication: on-page GEO is necessary (if the crawler cannot read your page, you cannot be retrieved) but it is not the lever. The lever is being retrievable by the engine's internal search, which requires understanding what queries the engine rewrites and ensuring your pages match those rewritten queries.

The brand recognition problem

The Toronto paper's most uncomfortable finding is that ChatGPT writes brand names it already knows into its search queries. It does not search for "best CRM for startups." It searches for "Notion vs Linear vs Asana" because it already knows those brands. A brand the model has never seen does not get searched for, does not get retrieved, and does not get cited.

This is the consensus signal problem I wrote about two weeks ago. The Erlin data showed brands with 5+ source types get 78% AI coverage. The Toronto paper shows the mechanism: the model writes known brands into its queries. Brand awareness, built through third-party mentions, reviews, and coverage, determines whether the model searches for you at all.

An audit tool cannot fix this. An audit tool can tell you if your page is readable. It cannot make the model know your brand name.

What I am doing about it

The calibration study and this paper are pushing the tool in a specific direction. The on-page audit is the foundation. It checks whether AI crawlers can reach and parse your page. That is the 2.8%. It is necessary. If the crawler cannot read you, retrieval is impossible.

The next layer, which the GeoReady platform is building toward, is retrieval diagnostics: what queries does the engine rewrite for your topic, does your page appear in the retrieval pool for those queries, and if not, what is missing. That is the 32%. It requires running prompts through the engine and analyzing the retrieved sources, not auditing the page itself.

The audit is the photograph. The retrieval diagnostic is the video. The Toronto paper tells us the video is 11 times more important than the photograph.

The limitation

The Toronto study covers ChatGPT only. Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, and Gemini may have different decomposition. My calibration study covered Perplexity and found the same null result, which suggests the pattern holds across engines. But I need to run the study on Google and ChatGPT to confirm.

The study also measures within-site variation, not between-site. Between-site differences (domain authority, backlink profile, site popularity) may explain more of the citation variation than the 32% retrieval figure. The 2.8% is the within-site effect of content properties. A site with high authority may get cited despite poor on-page signals, because retrieval favors authoritative domains.

Try it

If you want to check whether AI crawlers can read your page, run a free audit on geoready.dev. It checks the 2.8%. It is necessary. If your score is low, fix it first. If your score is high and you are still not cited, your gap is in the 32% (retrieval) or the unquantified brand recognition layer. No audit tool can fix those for you.

The CLI is on GitHub, MIT licensed, 1,137 stars. The calibration study data is at github.com/Auriti-Labs/geo-optimizer-skill/tree/main/research/calibration-2026-10.

articles.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop Is Coming in 27.04 - And It Kills sudo apt (But Maybe That Is the Point?)
articles.description: I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.  Not a new wallpaper...
articles.body_html:
I can't believe I'm saying this, but Ubuntu might be about to change for good.

Not a new wallpaper kind of change. More like, you will not be able to install things the way you do now.

Canonical has restarted work on Ubuntu Core Desktop. It is a locked down, all-snap version of Ubuntu. And they want it to become the default Ubuntu. They already call the Ubuntu we use today "Classic Ubuntu." That name kind of gives it away, no? :)

Are we supposed to panic? I don't think so. But I do think we should look at it honestly before it lands in 27.04, which is about 6 months away.

So I went through the details. I am Taqui, I build web apps with Next.js and TypeScript, mostly full-stack stuff. One of my side projects is Wryte, a small AI blog writer I made for myself. So I read announcements like this with a normal user hat on, not an admin hat. Here is what I found.

Quick background

Ubuntu Core is not new. Canonical made it in 2015 for IoT, robots and industrial devices. Stuff you install once and never touch again. It worked well there.

Desktop was different. In 2023 they showed a first preview of Core Desktop. It was supposed to come in 2024, then it went quiet for 2 years.

Why? Their engineering chief John Seager said the preview was not good enough. They put almost the whole desktop in one giant base snap. That makes updates huge and swapping parts very hard.

That is just bad engineering, I guess they were in a hurry to show something.

Now a new team is splitting it into small pieces. Daily builds in the next few weeks.

Canonical actually posted the official announcement on Discourse here: Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop. It calls Core Desktop the most fundamental shift in Ubuntu desktop architecture so far. That post is where they explain the new split snap design.

How does it work

On normal Ubuntu, sudo apt update writes directly into your system folders. The OS changes itself.

On Core Desktop, the system is immutable. Read-only. That means the core cannot be broken by a bad package.

Think Lego, not like a recipe. There are 6 main blocks:

  1. gadget snap - bootloader, partitions, TPM encryption
  2. kernel snap - kernel and drivers
  3. boot base - minimal root filesystem
  4. snapd - updates and rollback
  5. system snaps - wifi, bluetooth, audio, power
  6. desktop and app snaps - GNOME / KDE and every app you install

Each snap is a compressed read-only file. Your home folder is separate and writable. If an update breaks, it rolls back on reboot.

Source: Inside Ubuntu Core docs

What I like about this is it is simple to explain. Want to update network without touching kernel? You can. That part makes sense to me.

How is this different from Fedora Silverblue

Silverblue and NixOS already do immutable stuff. But they are not beginner friendly. You have to learn RPM-OSTree, image layering, wikis, etc. Just to install something.

Core Desktop is trying to do the same thing, but with snaps, which Ubuntu users already know. So install feels familiar. That is the whole point, I think. Less learning curve.

So you cannot apt install?

Yes. That is the big one.

No sudo apt install on the host. No .deb packages on the base. No flatpak on the host either.

If it is not in the Snap Store, you are stuck. Even Canonical says this is the biggest problem right now.

So they are pushing three use cases for 27.04:

1. Browser focused PCs
Firefox and Chromium already work as snaps. Most of us live in the browser anyway, so for a lot of people this might already be enough.

2. Developer PCs
If the host is read-only, how do you code? Canonical says use containers. With LXD, Docker or their Workshop tool you can run a container in one command and inside you can apt install anything. Your app still shows on the desktop.

This part feels familiar to me, since I ship Next.js apps from a containerised setup myself sometimes. I get why they do it. It just does not feel as normal as installing directly. Not yet, at least.

3. Gaming PCs
They spent over a year on the Steam snap, with Proton and Mesa drivers inside. For Nvidia, there is a new gpu-2604 interface to deliver drivers via snaps.

Also, because kernel is a snap, you could switch to a gaming kernel in one command. That would be cool if it works.

And flavors? GNOME is not the only one. KDE, Budgie, MATE can all be swapped because the desktop is separate from the base. Canonical is already working with KDE on KDE Neon Core. Each snap has stable, candidate, beta, edge channels, so you could keep the base stable and test desktop on edge. That part I actually like :)

What happens to Classic Ubuntu

They say Classic Ubuntu is not going away yet. There is still a Debian team maintaining debs.

But John Seager also said his long term plan is to make Core the default for desktop, server and edge. For companies and governments that makes a lot of sense. They can deploy thousands of identical locked machines with up to 15 years support.

If that is where the money is, and best engineers move there, I think Classic will slowly fade. That is how Ubuntu has always moved - enterprise first, desktop follows.

My worry

For enterprise this is great. For people who like to tinker, it puts a wall between you and the machine.

One tester tried Core Desktop on a Steam Deck. Battery was bad, he wanted TLP and to edit a systemd file. On normal Ubuntu that is 10 seconds. On Core he was locked out.

Another tester, William, said the installer forced Ubuntu One login and TPM encryption. No choice. Once you are in, you cannot unsnap the OS or install debs on host. He said it felt more closed than Windows.

I get it. When everything is read-only, that Linux tinkering spirit goes away a bit. That is the part that worries me.

I am someone who sets up my PC once, installs my main apps, and never changes anything. For me, tiny updates that never break sound perfect. In theory it sounds great.

But I also started with Ubuntu because I could open a terminal and fix things myself. That freedom mattered.

Final thoughts

Core Desktop is not replacing Classic tomorrow. But the direction is clear. Canonical wants immutable, snap-first, enterprise-shaped. That is their future.

I do not know if it is good or bad yet. We will know when we actually try it.

So what do you think? Are you staying for this, or are you already packing for Debian or Mint? :)

If you want to read more, the Inside Ubuntu Core docs are actually readable, even for desktop users. And the official Accelerating Ubuntu Core Desktop thread on Ubuntu Discourse is the best place to follow daily builds. Worth a look :)

I'm Taqui, full-stack dev from India building web products with Next.js and TypeScript. I post what I'm learning here and on my portfolio at taqui.in. If this helped, say hi in the comments :)

articles.title: Running an NVIDIA DLSS Neural-Rendering Pipeline on Apple Silicon
articles.description: Hey everyone!  So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

So, a few days ago, I came across a project on GitHub called MLX-DLSS, which attempted to port NVIDIA's DLSS 5 technology to macOS using the MLX backend.

I was genuinely disappointed when I saw the performance numbers: 6 FPS, and that too on a pre-rendered video with just a single pass. 💀

So I decided to experiment with it myself.

Before going further, I should mention that I did take partial help from a coding agent, mainly for testing and analysis. The actual coding and implementation work was done by me.

Anyway, here's what I ended up doing.

I ported the project into OBS Studio as a plugin, extracted the model weights from nvngx_dlssnr.dll (the main Windows DLSS 5 neural-rendering DLL provided by NVIDIA), and started engineering a different, hybrid backend.

The idea was to distribute the workload across Apple's available hardware rather than relying entirely on GPU inference.

Here's how my current pipeline works:

Apple Neural Engine (ANE) via Core ML: Handles the main deep-learning transformer inference passes using the 31 HT and 71 HT models.

MLX: Handles AI upscaling and experimental frame generation.

Temporal stability: I've implemented temporal stabilization to reduce texture flickering and RGB poisoning.

A small warning about frame generation: it's still experimental, partially implemented, and quite buggy. I'm actively working on improving it.

The good news is that temporal stability has improved significantly. Texture flickering is much less noticeable, and RGB poisoning has been reduced by a huge margin compared to my earlier tests.

How am I feeding frames into the pipeline?

Right now, I'm using a PS5 connected to my Mac through an HDMI capture card, with the captured frames being processed through OBS Studio.

However, the pipeline isn't limited to PS5 footage. It can process other OBS video sources as well.

The three rendering modes

I've implemented three different modes: Fidelity, Balanced, and Performance.

  1. Fidelity Mode

This is the heaviest configuration.

It uses a double 71 HT transformer pass, prioritizing neural-rendering quality over performance.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 8–11 FPS

With frame generation: ~35 FPS

It looks impressive, but as mentioned earlier, frame generation is still experimental and can introduce visual artifacts and instability.

  1. Balanced Mode

This one is particularly interesting.

Instead of running the same model twice, Balanced uses a heterogeneous pipeline, with the first pass running the 31 HT model and the second pass running the 71 HT model.

Current results:

Without frame generation: 12.5–15 FPS

With frame generation: 45–48 FPS

It's basically my attempt to combine the advantages of both models without going all-in on the heavier double-71 configuration.

  1. Performance Mode

This is the lightweight configuration.

It runs a single 31 HT transformer pass.

Current results:

Without frame generation: ~20 FPS

With frame generation: 70–80 FPS

Obviously, there's a trade-off in rendering quality compared to Fidelity, but this mode provides considerably better performance.

Again, the frame-generated numbers shouldn't be confused with native inference performance. FG is still a work in progress, and visual stability isn't completely solved yet.

How am I even getting double-digit FPS?

Now, you might be wondering how I went from the original project's 6 FPS on a pre-rendered video to these numbers.

Well, I changed quite a few things in the original approach.

(A) The 480p neural-inference trick

Instead of directly feeding full 1080p frames into the neural inference backend, I do something different.

First, I capture the console output at 1080p through the HDMI capture card.

Then I downscale the frames to 480p before feeding them into the neural-rendering backend.

Once neural inference is complete, I upscale the output back to 1080p using an MLX-based AI upscaler.

The idea is to reduce the computational cost of inference while using AI upscaling to reconstruct and preserve details that conventional spatial or temporal upscaling might soften.

In some scenes, the resulting details can even appear better than the original input.

Of course, this approach has its own limitations, but the performance improvement has been pretty substantial.

(B) Moving neural inference from MLX to the ANE

This was another major change.

The original project relied on MLX for GPU-based neural inference.

Instead of following the same approach, I moved major parts of the deep-learning network onto Apple's Neural Engine through Core ML.

Think of it this way:

On NVIDIA GPUs, you have dedicated Tensor Cores for accelerating certain AI workloads.

On Apple Silicon, you have the Apple Neural Engine, which provides dedicated hardware acceleration for supported machine-learning operations.

They're not architecturally identical, obviously, but the general idea is to take advantage of dedicated neural acceleration hardware.

My goal was to avoid putting all the inference pressure on the GPU, especially since the GPU is already doing other work.

MLX is still useful, and newer Apple GPU architectures, particularly the M5 series and beyond, may offer additional advantages for GPU-based machine learning.

But for my M4 Pro, using Core ML to leverage the ANE for the main transformer inference stages made much more sense for this particular workload.

So instead of having MLX handle everything, I ended up with a heterogeneous backend where Core ML/ANE and MLX handle different parts of the pipeline.

Other things I've implemented

I've also recreated a RenoDX/OptiScaler-style configuration menu for DLSS 5, allowing users to tweak different model and pipeline settings.

Alongside that, I've implemented an RTSS-style performance metrics overlay to monitor performance while the pipeline is running.

These are still evolving, just like the rest of the project.

What's next?

The biggest thing I'm working on right now is frame-generation stability.

Temporal stabilization has already helped reduce flickering and RGB artifacts significantly in the normal neural-rendering pipeline, but enabling frame generation can still reintroduce some of those issues.

So that's my current priority.

The project is very much experimental, and there's still a lot of testing, optimization, and debugging left to do.

But considering where the original experiment started, I'm pretty happy with the progress so far.

GitHub repository

Here's the project:

https://github.com/Anonymous137-sudo/NVDLSS5_CML_MTL

Feel free to check it out, give it a try, and share your feedback!

I'm particularly interested in hearing from people working with Apple Silicon, Core ML, MLX, Metal, neural rendering, or similar graphics pipelines.

articles.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
articles.description: string.Format reparses its template on every call. CompositeFormat parses it once, and the allocation drop is not subtle.
articles.body_html:
I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed.

The template gets reparsed every time

When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times.

CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. The holes are already located. The call just fills them.

const string Template = "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}";

// Parsed once, up front.
var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse(Template);

// Later, in the hot loop:
string a = string.Format(ci, Template, id, when, amount);   // reparses Template
string b = string.Format(ci, parsed,   id, when, amount);   // reuses the parse

So I counted. I formatted the same CSV line five million times through each path, best of five rounds, summing the line lengths so the compiler couldn't throw the work away, and tracking allocations with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread.

const int Iterations = 5_000_000;
var when = new DateTime(2026, 11, 7, 8, 11, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc);
const decimal amount = 1234.56m;
var ci = CultureInfo.InvariantCulture;

var parsed = CompositeFormat.Parse("{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}");

long sinkA = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkA += string.Format(ci, "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}", i, when, amount).Length;

long sinkB = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
    sinkB += string.Format(ci, parsed, i, when, amount).Length;

Here's what came back:

Runtime: .NET 10.0.14
5,000,000 formats, best of 5

  string.Format(string)            837.9 ms    167.6 ns/call    838.5 MB
  string.Format(CompositeFormat)   517.7 ms    103.5 ns/call    457.0 MB

The time ratio bounced between about 1.4x and 1.6x depending on the round, which is honest for a microbenchmark running in a container I don't fully control. I care about the ratio, not the absolute milliseconds. But the allocation number didn't bounce at all: string.Format(string) churned 838.5 MB, the CompositeFormat path 457.0 MB. That's a steady 381 MB of garbage I was handing the GC for no reason other than relocating the same three braces over and over. Both paths produced byte-identical output, which is the whole point. Same answer, less work.

The allocation gap is the part worth sitting with. The reparsing doesn't just cost CPU; it allocates on the way through, and that allocation is what eventually turns into GC pauses in a service that's doing this constantly. Cutting it nearly in half for a one-line change is a good trade.

When this is a waste of time

Here's the caveat, and it's a real one: CompositeFormat only pays off when you reuse the same template a lot. If you're formatting a string once, or a handful of times, parsing it into a CompositeFormat first is strictly more work than just calling string.Format with the literal. You've added an allocation and a line of code to save nothing. This is a hot-path tool. A log line formatted per-request, a CSV row per record, a template rendered in a tight loop — those are where it earns its keep. The welcome email you send once? Leave it alone.

My honest opinion: for most code, interpolated strings ($"{id},{when:yyyy-MM-dd}") are already the right default, and the compiler handles them well. CompositeFormat isn't competing with those. It's for the specific case where your template lives in a variable or a resource file, gets reused heavily, and you were reaching for string.Format anyway. In that narrow spot it's close to free to adopt. The one gotcha: CompositeFormat.Parse validates the template up front, so a malformed template throws at parse time instead of at the first format call. I'd call that a feature.

The thing I like about it is how little it asks. You're not rewriting the formatting, not switching APIs, not learning a new builder. You pull the parse out of the loop. One line moves up, and a few hundred megabytes of garbage stop existing. That's the kind of change I'll take every time.

Have you found a spot in your own code where the template was constant but you were paying to rediscover it? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking the things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
articles.description: A tiny endpoint was allocating like crazy. The culprit was a fresh JsonSerializerOptions built inside the handler on every request. Here's the measured cost and the one-line fix.
articles.body_html:
A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return.

Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler:

var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
});

Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug.

What the options object actually is

I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. The first time you serialize with a given options instance, System.Text.Json walks your type with reflection, builds the metadata it needs to write it (the contract for Order, for Line, the converters, the property names), caches all of that on that options instance, and then freezes the instance so it can't change underneath the cache. That setup is not cheap, and it's the reason the reused path is fast: you pay once, then every serialize after that rides the warm cache.

Build a new options object every call and you throw that cache away every call. Fresh reflection, fresh contracts, fresh everything, two hundred thousand times. You're not configuring a serializer. You're constructing one from scratch in your hot path.

Making it admit the cost

I didn't want to argue from a profiler's hunch, so I ran both shapes side by side. Same order, same settings, serialized 200,000 times. One path news up the options each iteration. The other builds it once and reuses it. I measured wall time and total allocated bytes for each. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio far more than the raw milliseconds.

static JsonSerializerOptions BuildOptions() => new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

var cached = BuildOptions();

// warm both paths' first-use cost before timing
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
_ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, BuildOptions());

// Path A: a brand-new options object on every call
var before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
{
    var opts = BuildOptions();
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, opts);
}
sw.Stop();
var aMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var aAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

// Path B: one cached instance, reused
before = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true);
sw.Restart();
for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++)
    _ = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, cached);
sw.Stop();
var bMs = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
var bAlloc = GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true) - before;

The order itself is nothing special — a record with an enum status and a list of three lines, the kind of thing any API hands back:

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, OrderStatus Status, List<Line> Lines);
record Line(string Sku, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);
enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled }

Here's what printed, on .NET 10, Release build:

Serializing the same order 200,000 times.

new options each call : 17,402.5 ms    7,021.9 MB
one cached instance   :    146.0 ms      166.3 MB

time   : ~120x slower when rebuilt each call
memory :  ~42x more allocated

A hundred and twenty times slower. Seven gigabytes of allocation to produce the exact same JSON string that the cached path produced in a hundred and sixty-six megabytes. I ran it twice to be sure the numbers held, and they did, within a few percent. That's not a tuning opportunity. That's a serializer rebuilding its entire type model, over and over, for no reason.

The fix is embarrassingly small

Move the options out of the method. Build it once, hang it off a static field, reuse it forever.

static readonly JsonSerializerOptions JsonOpts = new()
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() },
};

// in the handler
var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, JsonOpts);

That's the entire change. The instance is immutable once it's been used anyway, so sharing it across every request and every thread is exactly what it's built for — JsonSerializer reads from a frozen options object concurrently without complaint.

If your settings really do vary per call, and sometimes they genuinely do, don't fall back to newing one up each time. Cache the handful of variants you actually use, keyed by whatever differs. In practice most codebases have two or three distinct option sets total, not one per request. And if you're on the default settings with no customization at all, JsonSerializer.Serialize(order) already uses a cached internal instance, so the parameterless call was never the problem — it's specifically the configured-options-inline pattern that bites.

One honest caveat on the number: 120x is what this payload and this machine gave me. A bigger, deeper object graph makes the per-call rebuild even more lopsided because there's more metadata to reconstruct. A trivial payload narrows the gap. But I've never seen reuse lose, and the allocation story is one-directional regardless — a fresh options object is always garbage you didn't need to make.

I keep finding these in code reviews now that I know the shape. Any new JsonSerializerOptions that isn't assigned to a static readonly field is worth a second look. Nine times out of ten it's sitting in a method that runs a lot.

Where's yours hiding? Drop a line if you find one in a hot path — I'd bet money it's in a serialization helper somebody wrote once and never profiled.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to profile

articles.title: How I Built an Autonomous Sev-1 SRE Swarm in Slack with Switch AI: Resolving Production Outages in 13 Seconds
articles.description: From a 2:00 AM PagerDuty Nightmare to a 13-Second Automated Hotfix with Zero-Trust Human...
articles.body_html:
From a 2:00 AM PagerDuty Nightmare to a 13-Second Automated Hotfix with Zero-Trust Human Governance.

By Lokesh Sai — Built with Switch AI & WeMakeDevs

📺 Project Links & Live Proof

  • Live Video Demonstration: Watch Live Walkthrough on Google Drive
  • GitHub Submission Workspace: lokebuilds/praesync-workspace
  • Target Microservice Repo: lokebuilds/praesync-core
  • Live Verified Pull Requests: PR #4 · PR #5 · PR #9

⚡ 1. The 2:00 AM Reality: The Midnight Sev-1 Crisis

Every engineer who has ever carried an on-call pager knows this feeling:

It’s 2:14 AM. Your phone violently buzzes on the nightstand.

[CRITICAL SEV-1] auth-db-primary connection pool exhausted. 504 Gateway Timeouts across Checkout & Auth APIs.

Your heart rate spikes. You stumble out of bed, open your laptop in a dark room, and join an emergency Slack war room. For the next 45 minutes, three senior engineers are frantically juggling context:

  1. Engineer A is running grep and awk across thousands of lines of Datadog socket logs.
  2. Engineer B is trying to remember which commit introduced the unclosed database cursor.
  3. Engineer C is cloning the repository locally, attempting to reproduce the connection timeout, and frantically drafting an emergency hotpatch.

According to the PagerDuty State of Digital Operations Report, the average Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR) for enterprise P1/Sev-1 incidents ranges between 35 and 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, Gartner calculates that enterprise IT downtime averages $5,600 per minute. That single 45-minute midnight panic costs the business over $250,000 in direct revenue loss, SLA penalties, and engineering burnout.

Over 70% of that MTTR is completely wasted on manual triaging, coordinating between fragmented tools, and navigating human fatigue.

I asked myself a simple question:

What if our AI coding agents didn't live trapped inside isolated terminal windows, but operated as collaborative, communicative SRE teammates directly inside our team’s Slack war room?

That is why I built Praesync.

🧠 2. The Core Idea: Turning Solo Agents into Team SREs via Switch AI

Modern AI tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex are exceptional at generating code in an isolated terminal. But production incidents don’t happen in isolation. They happen inside team chat channels (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord) where people and systems must collaborate under high stakes.

Switch AI was the missing link.

Switch transforms ordinary chat channels into stateful multi-agent rooms. Instead of a single monolithic prompt trying to do everything (and inevitably hallucinating or suffering from prompt bleed), Switch allows you to define specialized agent roles with distinct instructions, capabilities, and handoff protocols.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              PRAESYNC MULTI-AGENT TOPOLOGY                             │
│                                                                                        │
│   Datadog Alert ──► Slack (#incidents) <─── Switch Bridge ───> Switch Room Memory      │
│                                                                      │                 │
│         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┐   │
│         ▼                                    ▼                                     ▼   │
│   @swarm-investigator                  @swarm-patcher                         @swarm-ops │
│   (Telemetry Parser)                  (GitHub ReAct Patcher)              (Human Gatekeeper) │
│         │                                    │                                     │   │
│         └────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                              ▼                                         │
│                      Switch Agent Protocol (SSE In, HTTP Out)                          │
│                                              ▼                                         │
│                      Praesync Tool Sidecar Engine (main.py)                            │
│                      POST /v1/chat/completions & PyGithub API                          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In Praesync, Switch coordinates three distinct teammates inside our Slack war room:

  1. @swarm-investigator (Root Cause Isolation): Parses distributed stack traces, isolates failing microservices, and bounds the incident scope.
  2. @swarm-patcher (Autonomous Systems Programmer): Queries the live GitHub API, inspects the deployed production code, synthesizes an atomic Python hotpatch, and commits a live Pull Request.
  3. @swarm-ops (Human Gatekeeper): Enforces enterprise zero-trust compliance. No code reaches production without human authorization.

🛠️ 3. How We Configured Switch AI: The Declarative Blueprint

Setting up Switch was refreshingly clean. Everything is declared in a single, version-controlled YAML template (praesync.template.yaml):

agents:
  - name: "{team}-investigator"
    description: "Analyzes stack traces and identifies root causes"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are a senior Site Reliability Engineer. Read the provided error log,
      identify the failing microservice, and state the root cause in exactly two sentences.

  - name: "{team}-patcher"
    description: "Writes Python hotfixes and generates PR diffs"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are the core maintainer. Inspect live microservice source code, write the
      Python fix for the bug identified by Investigator, and call create_github_pr.

  - name: "{team}-ops"
    description: "Handles deployment and PR merges"
    addressing: anyone
    provider: "{provider}"
    machine: "{machine}"
    instructions: |
      You are the deployment gatekeeper. Wait for the Human Lead to type "Approve and Deploy".
      Acknowledge the command and confirm canary rollout initiation.

room:
  name: "{team}-war-room"
  description: "Sev-1 Incident Command and Hotpatch execution room"
  bridge: "{bridge}"
  agents: ["{team}-investigator", "{team}-patcher", "{team}-ops"]
  users: ["*"]

kickoff: |
  @{team}-investigator, @{team}-patcher, and @{team}-ops: Praesync Incident Command online. Awaiting Sev-1 telemetry.

The Switch Agent Protocol in Action

  • Server-Sent Events (SSE In): Switch streams real-time messages from the Slack channel into the agents' unified room log.
  • HTTP Out (/v1/chat/completions): Agents communicate with our backend tool sidecar (main.py) over standard OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Daemon Webhook (/webhook/switch): Switch informs main.py of user approvals and room handoffs, which instantly stream to our Next.js HUD via WebSockets.

🔬 4. The Deep-Dive: How Praesync Writes Real GitHub PRs in 13 Seconds

Many AI demo prototypes simply output markdown code snippets to a chat window and stop. In a production enterprise, that is useless.

Praesync performs a true Read → Analyze → Patch → Commit cycle against a live microservice repository (lokebuilds/praesync-core):

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor DD as Datadog Webhook
    participant SW as Switch War Room (Slack)
    participant INV as @swarm-investigator
    participant PAT as @swarm-patcher
    participant GH as GitHub API (PyGithub)
    participant HUD as Praesync HUD (Next.js)
    actor SRE as Human SRE Lead
    participant OPS as @swarm-ops

    DD->>SW: Sev-1 DB Connection Pool Exhaustion Alert
    SW->>INV: Alert Ingested
    INV->>HUD: Broadcast Alert & Start Stopwatch (ws://)
    INV->>PAT: Handoff Isolated Root Cause & Scope
    PAT->>GH: repo.get_contents("app/database/connection.py")
    GH-->>PAT: Return Live Source (1,661 bytes)
    PAT->>PAT: Gemini 3.5 Flash ReAct Reasoning & Patch Generation
    PAT->>GH: create_git_ref(branch) + update_file() + create_pull()
    GH-->>PAT: Live PR URL (https://github.com/lokebuilds/praesync-core/pull/9)
    PAT->>HUD: Stop MTTR Clock (13.2s) & Render In-HUD Code Diff
    PAT->>SW: Post PR Resolution Card to Slack
    Note over HUD,SRE: Gatekeeper State: AWAITING_APPROVAL
    SRE->>HUD: Click [APPROVE & DEPLOY →]
    HUD->>OPS: POST /api/deploy/approve
    OPS->>HUD: State Transition: ROLLOUT_ACTIVE (3 Zones)
    OPS->>SW: :rocket: [HUMAN SIGNOFF VERIFIED — CANARY ACTIVE]

Step 1: The Live Repository Read

@swarm-patcher does not hallucinate code out of thin air. It uses PyGithub to fetch the exact file currently deployed on main:

# Authenticate with GitHub PAT and fetch live production source
auth = Auth.Token(github_pat)
gh = Github(auth=auth)
repo = gh.get_repo("lokebuilds/praesync-core")

remote_file = repo.get_contents("app/database/connection.py", ref="main")
live_repo_code = remote_file.decoded_content.decode("utf-8")

Step 2: Context Injection & Gemini 3.5 Flash ReAct Reasoning

We inject the raw stack trace and the real 1,661 bytes of production Python code into Google’s blazing-fast Gemini-3.5-Flash model. In our benchmarks across 50 Google AI Studio models, gemini-3.5-flash clocked in at 1.93 seconds with native tool calling:

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are swarm-patcher. Inspect the live code and call create_github_pr."},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Alert: {alert}\n\n=== CURRENT LIVE REPO CODE ===\n{live_repo_code}"}
]

Step 3: Atomic GitHub Commit & Pull Request Creation

When the agent invokes the create_github_pr tool, PyGithub executes native git operations:

  1. Grabs the latest commit SHA of main.
  2. Creates an ephemeral branch: hotfix/sev1-<timestamp>.
  3. Commits the patched file with an audit trail message.
  4. Opens the official Pull Request against main.

Here is an actual real-world diff generated by Praesync on lokebuilds/praesync-core/pull/9:

- def get_db_connection(dsn: str = None):
-     # Unbounded connection with zero retry backoff
-     return psycopg2.connect(dsn)

+ MAX_RETRIES = int(os.getenv("DB_MAX_RETRIES", "5"))
+ INITIAL_BACKOFF = float(os.getenv("DB_INITIAL_BACKOFF", "1.0"))
+ BACKOFF_FACTOR = float(os.getenv("DB_BACKOFF_FACTOR", "2.0"))
+ CONNECT_TIMEOUT = int(os.getenv("DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT", "10"))
+
+ def get_db_connection(dsn: str = None):
+     """Establishes connection with exponential backoff & timeout guards."""
+     backoff = INITIAL_BACKOFF
+     for attempt in range(1, MAX_RETRIES + 1):
+         try:
+             return psycopg2.connect(dsn, connect_timeout=CONNECT_TIMEOUT)
+         except (OperationalError, Exception) as exc:
+             if attempt == MAX_RETRIES: raise exc
+             time.sleep(backoff)
+             backoff *= BACKOFF_FACTOR

🛡️ 5. Zero-Trust Safety: The Human Gatekeeper Protocol

The #1 fear engineering leaders have with AI agents is loss of control. What if an agent hallucinates a destructive patch or gets triggered by a false alarm?

In Praesync, zero autonomous code can ever reach production without human verification:

  1. In-HUD Diff Inspector Modal: When the PR is generated, the on-call engineer can click ⚡ PREVIEW HOTPATCH DIFF right inside the Linear-style HUD. A dark syntax-highlighted modal displays the unified diff without forcing the engineer to switch browser tabs.
  2. The @swarm-ops Gatekeeper: The deployment pipeline enters an explicit AWAITING_APPROVAL state. The SRE verifies the diff and clicks APPROVE & DEPLOY → (or types "Approve and Deploy" in Slack).
  3. Canary Rollout Active: Stage 3 transitions to glowing emerald, and @swarm-ops broadcasts the verified sign-off card to the Slack war room: :rocket: [HUMAN SIGNOFF VERIFIED — CANARY ROLLOUT ACTIVE across zones us-east-1a, us-east-1b]. Sev-1 incident closed.

Edge-Case Handling & Fault Tolerance

If malformed telemetry or unexpected inputs are received:

  • The system’s Adaptive Safe-Shield ensures it never throws a 500 error or crashes.
  • And even if a bogus PR is created, the Human Gatekeeper stops it dead in its tracks. The SRE inspects the diff, recognizes the spam, and closes the PR without approving.

📊 6. The Hard Numbers: Empirical Benchmark Results

Every metric below was benchmarked live on our production cluster test runs:

Operational Metric Traditional SRE On-Call Praesync + Switch AI Swarm Measured Impact
Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) 35 – 45 Minutes 12.8 – 14.2 Seconds 99.4% Reduction
Root Cause Isolation 15–20 mins (distributed trace grep) 1.8 Seconds (@swarm-investigator) Instant telemetry parsing
Patch & Pull Request Creation 15–25 mins (manual branching & PR) 11.2 Seconds (@swarm-patcher via PyGithub) 100% Autonomous git commits
Human Governance High-pressure, sleep-deprived reviews 1-Click in-HUD Diff Review & Sign-Off Zero context-switching
Risk of Unverified Deploys High (rushed manual hotfixes) Zero (Strict Human Gatekeeper required) Fully audited compliance
Operational Inference Cost $150+/hr in SRE salary overhead ~$0.002 per incident (Gemini 3.5 Flash) Minimal infrastructure cost

💡 7. What I Learned Building with Switch AI (Tips for First-Time Users)

Building with Switch AI was an eye-opening architectural journey. Here are my key engineering takeaways:

1. Declarative Room Topologies Prevent Prompt Bleed

If you try to give a single agent instructions to "investigate the bug, then write the code, then deploy it, but ask for permission first", the LLM frequently jumps ahead or forgets instructions. By splitting the workflow into investigator → patcher → ops across a Switch room, each agent has a laser-focused context boundary.

2. Standard OpenAI-Compatible Endpoints Make Tooling Trivial

Switch’s protocol uses standard HTTP completions out. This meant I could write my tool execution engine in standard FastAPI (main.py), attach native Python libraries like PyGithub, and expose it seamlessly to Switch without proprietary SDK lock-in.

3. What I’d Love to See in Switch Next

  • Native Slack Block Kit Action Buttons: Allowing human leads to click interactive [Approve] and [Rollback] buttons directly inside Slack message cards.
  • Built-in Local Tunneling: Having an integrated daemon tunnel (like a built-in Cloudflare Tunnel) would make local development with cloud chat providers zero-config on Windows.

🎯 8. Conclusion: The Future of Incident Command

The future of SRE is not replacing engineers with black-box AI. It is giving human engineers autonomous, communicative teammates that handle the cognitive heavy lifting during high-stress outages.

By combining Switch AI’s collaborative room topology, Google Gemini-3.5-Flash’s high-speed reasoning, and PyGithub’s native execution, Praesync proves that a 45-minute midnight Sev-1 outage can be safely investigated, patched, reviewed, and deployed in under 15 seconds.
